---
title: "Is there a correlation? (solutions)"
format: html
---

Teacher version. Chunks run. The penguins come with the palmerpenguins package, so no data file is needed.

```{r}
#| label: setup
pacman::p_load(here, tidyverse, palmerpenguins)
```

## The question

Is there a correlation? Two continuous variables: when one goes up, what does the other do? A scatter plot draws one point for each row. The x position is one variable and the y position is the other.

## 1. The scatter plot

Run the chunk and read the message from R. `Removed 2 rows`: 2 penguins have no flipper length or no body mass.

```{r}
#| label: first-scatter
penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point()
```

`!is.na()` keeps penguins with both measurements. The points rise to the right: penguins with longer flippers weigh more.

```{r}
#| label: fixed-scatter
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point()
```

### Your turn 1

Draw flipper length (x) against bill length (y).

```{r}
#| label: turn-1
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(bill_length_mm)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point()
```

Answer: longer. The points rise to the right (correlation 0.66), with two groups visible: a cloud at the bottom left and a cloud at the top right.

## 2. One color for each species

`color = species` gives each species its own color.

```{r}
#| label: color-species
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point()
```

### Your turn 2

Color the flipper and bill length plot by species.

```{r}
#| label: turn-2
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(bill_length_mm)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point()
```

Answer: `species`. Gentoo has the longest flippers (217 mm on average). Adelie has the shortest bills (38.8 mm on average).

## 3. A line through the points

`geom_smooth()` adds a line. Run the chunk and read the message. `using method = 'loess'`: R drew a curve that bends with the data. The grey band shows the uncertainty of the curve.

```{r}
#| label: smooth-default
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth()
```

`method = "lm"` draws a straight line. The line shows how much y changes when x goes up by one unit. Here we get one line for each species.

```{r}
#| label: smooth-lm
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

To get one line for all penguins, move `color` into `geom_point()`. A `color` inside `ggplot()` applies to every layer. A `color` inside `geom_point()` applies to the points only.

```{r}
#| label: smooth-one-line
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

### Your turn 3

Add one straight line to the flipper and bill length plot. Keep the colors on the points.

```{r}
#| label: turn-3
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(bill_length_mm)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

Answer: `lm`. The line rises 0.26 mm of bill for each extra millimeter of flipper.

## 4. One panel for each species

`facet_wrap(~ species)` draws one panel for each species.

```{r}
#| label: facet
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  facet_wrap(~ species)
```

### Your turn 4

Draw the flipper and bill length plot with one panel for each species.

```{r}
#| label: turn-4
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(bill_length_mm)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  facet_wrap(~ species)
```

Answer: `species`. Gentoo is steepest (0.31 mm of bill per mm of flipper) and Adelie is flattest (0.13). Chinstrap is in between (0.22).

## 5. When the groups change the story (optional)

Bill depth against flipper length, with one line for all penguins. The line goes down.

```{r}
#| label: depth-one-line
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(bill_depth_mm)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

One line for each species. Inside every species the line goes up.

```{r}
#| label: depth-species
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(bill_depth_mm)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

### Your turn 5

Facet the bill depth plot by species. Which line is steepest?

```{r}
#| label: turn-5
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm), !is.na(bill_depth_mm)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  facet_wrap(~ species)
```

Answer: `species`. Gentoo is steepest (0.11 mm of depth per mm of flipper), then Chinstrap (0.09) and Adelie (0.06).

## Notes for the teacher

- Correlation between flipper length and body mass: 0.87. Flipper length and bill length: 0.66. Flipper length and bill depth: -0.58.
- Slopes in grams of body mass per mm of flipper: all penguins 49.7, Adelie 32.8, Chinstrap 34.6, Gentoo 54.6.
- Slopes in mm of bill length per mm of flipper: all penguins 0.26, Adelie 0.13, Chinstrap 0.22, Gentoo 0.31.
- Slopes in mm of bill depth per mm of flipper: all penguins -0.08, Adelie 0.06, Chinstrap 0.09, Gentoo 0.11. The sign flips because Gentoo has the longest flippers and the shallowest bills.
- `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` prints `using formula = 'y ~ x'`. The message is harmless. Students can ignore it.
- If time runs short, section 5 becomes homework.
